title: The old rehatnamas
hook: earlier codes differ in detail; the 1950 code is the shared reference

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sarbat Khalsa: the whole panth gathered to decide as one. Your line was all of us together. Did you ask the quietest person, and what did they say? Day one thousand two hundred eighty-five.

Two recipe cards for the same dish. One in a grandmother's hand, splattered, with a note in the margin. One printed in a community cookbook, neat and measured. The dish is the same dish. But one card says a handful and the other says a cup, and one adds a spice the other never mentions. Which is right? Families have that argument at holiday tables. Sikhs have a version of it too, written down over generations. Before the shared code we have been reading for weeks now, there were older ones, and they don't all say the same thing. Today we open that older shelf.
screen: `TWO CARDS, ONE DISH.` → `A HANDFUL OR A CUP?` → `AN OLDER SHELF OF CODES.`

segments.voice: A rehatnama is a writing about rehat, the Sikh way of living. In the generations after the Tenth Guru, Sikhs wrote several of these. Some carry the names of people tradition places near the Guru, such as the poet Bhai Nand Lal. They set out how a Sikh should rise, pray, dress, eat and treat others. Read them side by side and you find a lot of common ground: remember the Name, keep the hair, live honestly, share. Read them closely and you find differences. One stresses a rule another leaves out. Some carry the worries and the language of the time and place they were written in. Who wrote which parts, and when, is still discussed, and that question is still open. So, much later, Sikh bodies worked together to agree on one shared code, and the result is the Sikh Rehat Maryada we have been walking through, published by the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee. Today it is the shared reference gurdwaras point to, though some groups and some historic places keep customs of their own beside it. Here's the turn. Codes are the community's best written understanding of how to live the Guru's way, and the way they are written can change from one era to the next. The Guru they are trying to follow does not. The Guru Granth Sahib is fixed, word for word. Every code, old or new, is measured against it, never the other way round. Codes change, the guru doesn't.
screen: `A REHATNAMA: A WRITING ON REHAT.` · `COMMON GROUND, DIFFERENT DETAILS.` · `ONE SHARED CODE AGREED LATER.` · `EVERY CODE MEASURED BY THE GRANTH.` · then, large: `CODES CHANGE, THE GURU DOESN'T.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read two versions of one rule. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a rule you've heard said two ways. Maybe your family's version and a book's version. Maybe how a teacher said it and how a parent did. Hold both side by side. Where do they agree? Where do they differ? Then ask what both are trying to protect. Stay with that thing, the one underneath the two wordings, until the bell. The bell holds the time.
The old rehatnamas. Earlier writings on the Sikh way of life, sharing much and differing in detail, before the shared code was agreed. Today's word.
Your line: codes change, the guru doesn't. Today, when a rule annoys you, ask what it's protecting before you decide what to do with it. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: Sikh scholars study the older rehatnamas alongside the Sikh Rehat Maryada, which serves as the shared reference for Sikh conduct today.
